column4: The section names 89:4 يَسْرِ as night walking; 17:1 uses أَسْرَىٰ … لَيْلًا for God carrying His servant by night, giving the image a divinely directed night journey.
The section's root note on 89:4 is night travel; here Lot's household is ordered to leave at night (فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ بِقِطْعٍ مِّنَ ٱلَّيْلِ), a second, urgent night departure.
The section's night-walking note meets Lot's departure: the command فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ بِقِطْعٍ مِّنَ ٱلَّيْلِ sets a family on the road before dawn.
The section names the root س ر ي for night travel; Moses is told أَنْ أَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي, so the root becomes a collective escape route from Pharaoh.
The section's night-walking root recurs in the command أَنْ أَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي; this is Moses leading the people away while pursuit is expected.
The section's root note on 89:4 is enacted in أَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي لَيْلًا: a night departure that carries the people toward safety while they are pursued.
The section's travel-worn mount becomes a concrete Quranic transport scene: livestock carry burdens to a distant بلد that people could reach only with hardship (بِشِقِّ الْأَنفُسِ).
The preceding 16:7 gives beasts carrying burdens over a hard journey; this ayah names horses, mules, and donkeys made for riding, expanding the section's mount image.
The section hears a road-worn she-camel beside its account of testing; the pilgrimage call brings people on foot and on every lean camel (ضَامِرٍ), a specific arduous journey by mount.

The section sets night travel and settling in place against one another; this ayah describes animal-skin dwellings made light for the day of travel and the day of stopping (ظَعْنِكُمْ … إِقَامَتِكُمْ), a portable answer to becoming fixed.
The section's road across lands meets the description of earth as a resting-place with paths placed through it (سُبُلًا لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ): earth is made traversable and gives direction.
The section joins a mount to the return journey; the following ayat develop that scene, and this ayah supplies the animals and ships made into means of transport.
After 43:12 names mounts, this ayah has riders settle on their backs and remember their Lord (عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهَا); it joins travel with acknowledgment at the moment of riding.
The section's road ends in return to the Lord; after describing the mount, this ayah says إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا لَمُنقَلِبُونَ, explicitly making the ride a reminder of return.

The section contrasts walking with clinging to earth; this ayah makes earth traversable (فَامْشُوا فِي مَنَاكِبِهَا), provides sustenance, and ends with resurrection to God, linking road, provision, and destination.
The section's earth can be a weight that holds a person down; this ayah instead says God spread it out (بِسَاطًا), and 71:20 gives the purpose: people travel its broad routes.
The section pictures a person stuck to earth; this continuation says earth was spread so people may travel its broad ways (سُبُلًا فِجَاجًا), turning the same ground into a route.

The section itself names this reverse arrangement: ثَاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ is being heavy toward earth, followed by the question whether they prefer worldly life to the Hereafter, opposite the journey to God.
The section itself cites أَخْلَدَ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ وَاتَّبَعَ هَوَاهُ: remaining attached to earth and following desire makes the earth-bound person the direct counter-image of the traveler.

The section's 9:38 image makes people heavy and fixed toward earth; this command reverses it with انْفِرُوا خِفَافًا وَثِقَالًا, calling them to go forth in either condition and strive with wealth and selves.
The section likens attachment to a mount that will not rise; this ayah explicitly distinguishes those who stay seated (الْقَاعِدُونَ) from those who strive with their lives and property.

The section's beloved wealth pins a person in place; these stay-behinds say their property and families occupied them (شَغَلَتْنَا أَمْوَالُنَا وَأَهْلُونَا), making attachment the stated reason they did not travel.
The section hears travel wearing down a mount; this ayah names thirst, fatigue, hunger, and every step taken in God's path as real costs that are counted as good deeds.

The section's dictionary image of a travel-worn mount has a human counterpart: after their journey Moses and his companion say, لَقَدْ لَقِينَا مِن سَفَرِنَا هَٰذَا نَصَبًا, describing the journey's fatigue.

The section's b ل و note pictures a journey wearing down what seems one's own; this ayah says believers will be tested in their property and selves (لَتُبْلَوُنَّ فِي أَمْوَالِكُمْ وَأَنفُسِكُمْ), making the test reach possessions directly.
The section links the root ب ل و to what a person thinks is theirs; this ayah calls property and children a test (أَمْوَالُكُمْ وَأَوْلَادُكُمْ فِتْنَةٌ) and points beyond them to God's reward.
The section's test image reaches what people possess; this repeated formulation calls property and children a trial (فِتْنَةٌ) and sets God's great reward beyond them.
The section's b ل و note says testing can wear down what a person claims as his own; this ayah specifies fear, hunger, and loss of property, lives, and produce as tests.
The preceding 2:155 lists losses in the test; this ayah gives the afflicted people's own response, إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ, joining trial to return.
The section connects being tested with the road back to God; this ayah says people are tested with good and evil (نَبْلُوكُم بِالشَّرِّ وَالْخَيْرِ) and ends, وَإِلَيْنَا تُرْجَعُونَ.
The section says the road-worn mount and return call meet in one person; this ayah makes the human the traveler, كَادِحٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ كَدْحًا, laboring toward the Lord and meeting Him.
The section's dictionary note calls مَعَاد a place of return; this ayah promises the Prophet, لَرَادُّكَ إِلَىٰ مَعَادٍ, a return to the appointed destination.
The section says ر ج ع is going back to where one began; this ayah joins God beginning creation, repeating it, and people's return to Him (ثُمَّ إِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ).
The section describes the road's end as a place of settling; this ayah names the final resting-place as إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمُسْتَقَرُّ.
The section names return to the Lord as the destination; this ayah states it as an unavoidable endpoint: إِنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ الرُّجْعَىٰ.
The section explains the tranquil soul through stillness after disturbance and cites this source: remembrance of God is what makes hearts tranquil (تَطْمَئِنُّ الْقُلُوبُ).

The section's root note defines tranquility as calm after disturbance; Abraham asks to see how God gives life so his heart may be reassured (لِيَطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبِي), a specific arrival at settled certainty.
The preceding 13:28 explains tranquil hearts; this ayah adds the believers' blessed state and good return (حُسْنُ مَآبٍ), joining inward rest to a destination.
The section's love image is attachment to money; the oath-surah says a person is intense in love of wealth (لِحُبِّ الْخَيْرِ لَشَدِيدٌ), a direct formulation of that attachment.

The section compares clinging to wealth with a mount that will not move; this ayah names family, property, and trade as more beloved than God, His Messenger, and striving in His path, making attachment the reason for staying back.
The section focuses on love of wealth; this ayah lists gold, silver, and other desired possessions as attractions of worldly life, then sets the better return with God beyond them.
The section says a person can cling to wealth as though it were his own; the garden-owner boasts that he has more wealth (أَكْثَرُ مِنكَ مَالًا), giving that attachment a concrete speaker.

The preceding 18:34 gives the wealthy owner's boast; this ayah shows him entering his garden while wronging himself and denying that it will ever perish, exposing the false permanence of what he owns.

The section names return to the Lord as the true destination; the wealthy owner imagines, وَلَئِن رُّدِدتُّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّي, that even a return would bring him something better, reversing humble return into entitlement.
The preceding garden narrative shows a man trusting his wealth; this ayah says the crop is destroyed and he wrings his hands over what he spent, a concrete case of possessions passing away.
The section's loved wealth is something people cling to; this ayah calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life, then says lasting good deeds are better with the Lord.
The section's intense love of money is made concrete in the person who gathers wealth and counts it (جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ).

The section joins attachment to wealth with heaviness toward earth; Qarun's treasure is so vast that its keys weigh on a company of strong men (لَتَنُوءُ بِالْعُصْبَةِ), a specific image of riches as burden.

The preceding 28:76 describes Qarun's immense treasure; this ayah says the earth swallowed him and his dwelling (فَخَسَفْنَا بِهِ وَبِدَارِهِ الْأَرْضَ), making wealth's weight a literal collapse into earth.
The section's money-lover remains attached to what he has; this ayah says rivalry in accumulation (التَّكَاثُرُ) distracts people, naming the force that keeps them occupied.
The preceding 102:1 names distraction by accumulation; this ayah carries it to the graves (حَتَّىٰ زُرْتُمُ الْمَقَابِرَ), giving attachment a finite endpoint.
The section calls entry the last stage of the journey; this ayah shows the God-fearing being led in groups to the Garden (إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ زُمَرًا) and welcomed at its open gates.

The section's final movement is entry into the Garden; this neighboring passage says the Garden is brought near to the God-fearing (أُزْلِفَتِ الْجَنَّةُ), depicting arrival before the invitation in 50:34.
The section describes return and entry; this ayah identifies the promised Garden as the outcome for every returning, watchful person (أَوَّابٍ حَفِيظٍ), joining return to the destination.
The preceding 50:32 speaks of every returning person; this ayah describes one who comes with a heart returning to God (قَلْبٍ مُّنِيبٍ), the inward counterpart of the section's tranquil soul.
The section ends with a command to enter among God's servants; this ayah gives the Garden's arrival command, ادْخُلُوهَا بِسَلَامٍ, and names it the day of abiding.
The section's last stage is entry; this ayah gives the Garden's direct welcome, ادْخُلُوهَا بِسَلَامٍ آمِنِينَ, marking safe arrival.
The section's r ج ع note describes a return to the beginning-place; at death the denier instead begs, رَبِّ ارْجِعُونِ, to be sent back into worldly life, the opposite direction.
The preceding 23:99 is a plea to return; this ayah answers with كَلَّا, the same response word the section notes in Surah 89, and says the plea will not reopen the completed journey.
The section's return-call brings the soul to the Lord; these condemned people instead ask, رَبَّنَا أَخِّرْنَا, for more earthly time to act, reversing the final return into a request to delay it.
The preceding 32:12 asks for delay; this ayah answers that the decision is settled and that Hell will be filled, giving the refusal that completes the failed request to return.

The section contrasts the tranquil soul's return with the denier's rejected request; here the condemned ask to be brought out so they can act righteously, and are told they had ample life and warning.
The section's return is the road's endpoint; this ayah gives a dying person the opposite wish, رَبِّ لَوْلَا أَخَّرْتَنِي, hoping for more time to give charity and become righteous.
The preceding 63:10 asks for delay; this ayah says God will not delay a soul when its term arrives, a boundary on the wish to resume the journey.

The section names Thamud cutting rock and refers to lands where people settle; this speech recalls their settlement after Aad and their carving houses from mountains (تَنْحِتُونَ الْجِبَالَ بُيُوتًا), a direct rock-and-dwelling parallel.
This passage opens with the people of the rocky dwellings (أَصْحَابَ الْحِجْرِ), the community whose mountain-cut houses continue the section's Thamud rock scene in 15:82.
The section names Thamud as people who cut rock; this ayah says the people of the Hijr carved houses from mountains (يَنْحِتُونَ مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا).
After 15:82 shows the carved mountain houses, this ayah says the people were seized by the cry in the morning, carrying the settled rock-city scene into its end.
The preceding passage gives the carved dwellings and their destruction; this ayah says what they had earned did not avail them, linking the old settlement to the section's warning about possessions.
The section's Thamud scene centers on cutting rock; this ayah says they carved houses from mountains with skill and pride (تَنْحِتُونَ مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا فَارِهِينَ).

The section's b ل و note evokes a she-camel worn by travel, while this ayah sends Thamud a she-camel as a test (النَّاقَةِ فِتْنَةً لَّهُمْ); the shared animal and trial meet in a distinct Quranic scene.
The section names Thamud and develops a camel image beside testing; this ayah recalls that Thamud received the she-camel as a clear sign but wronged it, joining the named people, camel, and test.
The section names Thamud and connects testing with a female camel; this ayah says Thamud denied the truth in their transgression (بِطَغْوَاهَا), setting the camel episode in its moral context.
The preceding ayah names Thamud's transgression; this ayah says their most wretched man sprang forward, the act that leads into the warning about the she-camel in 91:13.
The section's camel is a travel-worn mount, while this continuation names Allah's she-camel and its allotted drink (نَاقَةَ اللَّهِ وَسُقْيَاهَا), a distinct but specific camel scene among Thamud.
The preceding 91:13 sets the she-camel boundary; this ayah says they denied and hamstrung her, after which their Lord destroyed them, connecting the Thamud scene to the section's doomed old powers.
The section says Pharaoh's stake (أَوْتَاد) pins a foot to earth; this ayah repeats the specific title فِرْعَوْنُ ذُو الْأَوْتَادِ in the account of earlier deniers.
The section's peg image is a human stake driven into the ground; this ayah calls mountains pegs (أَوْتَادًا), shifting the same fastening image from Pharaoh's power to the created landscape.
In the continuing story of Aad, this ayah asks whether they build a sign on every high place (آيَةً بِكُلِّ رِيعٍ), recalling the monumental landscape beside Iram's pillars in the section.
The section's old cities seem fixed and enduring; Aad's people take fortresses (مَصَانِعَ) as if they might abide forever, a direct false-permanence parallel to the journey's eventual end.
The section says earlier peoples transgressed in the lands; this ayah describes Aad's violence as tyrannical whenever they seized someone (بَطَشْتُم بَطَشْتُمْ جَبَّارِينَ).
The section names Aad and says earlier peoples transgressed in the lands; this ayah says Aad became arrogant on earth without right (اسْتَكْبَرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ الْحَقِّ).
The preceding 41:15 describes Aad's arrogance on earth; this ayah gives the destructive wind sent against them, a specific outcome for the land-transgressors named in the section.
The section also names Thamud; this ayah turns to them, says they preferred blindness to guidance, and describes the humiliating thunderbolt that seized them.
The section names both Aad and Thamud and their settled lands; this ayah names the same peoples, points to their dwellings, and says Satan turned them from the path despite their insight.
The section names Aad and Thamud among the settled powers; this ayah names both together (ثَمُودُ وَعَادٌ) in the account of the overwhelming blow against earlier deniers.
The preceding 69:4 names Thamud and Aad; this ayah specifies Thamud's destruction by the overwhelming blast, completing one side of the section's paired peoples.
The preceding passage names Aad; this ayah gives their destruction by a furious wind (بِرِيحٍ صَرْصَرٍ), a concrete fate for one of the section's old powers.
The preceding 69:6 names the wind against Aad; this ayah describes it lasting seven nights and eight days and leaving people fallen, extending the scene of their disappearance.
After the wind account against Aad, this ayah asks whether any remnant of them is seen, making the ruined power and empty land explicit.
The section's earth is heavy and is crushed at the journey's end; this ayah gives the contrary end-time scene of the earth being stretched out (مُدَّتِ الْأَرْضُ).
The preceding 84:3 spreads the earth; this ayah says it throws out what is within and empties itself, continuing the collapse of the settled ground.
The preceding verses describe the earth laid bare; this ayah says it listens to its Lord's command, turning the land itself toward the final summons.
The section links a person to earth's weight and final crushing; this ayah reverses stable ground into earth shaken by its quake (زُلْزِلَتِ الْأَرْضُ زِلْزَالَهَا).
The preceding 99:1 shakes the earth; this ayah says it brings out its burdens (أَثْقَالَهَا), making the earth's weight and release a direct continuation.
After the earth shakes and releases its burdens, this ayah gives humanity's startled question about what has happened to it, the human response to the upheaval.
The preceding verses establish the earth's shaking and humanity's question; this ayah says the earth will report its news, making the ground disclose what it carried.
The preceding 99:4 says the earth will speak; this ayah says its Lord inspired it, completing the scene of earth answering the final command.

The section's root note defines tranquility as settling after disturbance; after the prescribed prayer in fear, this ayah says when people become secure (اطْمَأْنَنتُمْ), they return to regular prayer.
The section's tranquil soul returns to its Lord; these people are satisfied with worldly life and settled into it (اطْمَأَنُّوا بِهَا), making worldly repose the opposite of the final repose.

The section's soul is tranquil at the journey's end; this ayah describes a person who is reassured only when good comes (اطْمَأَنَّ بِهِ) and turns back when tested, a conditional and unstable counterpart.
The section's final caravan enters the Garden in 39:73; this verse gives the opposing procession, disbelievers driven in groups toward Hell.
The preceding 39:71 shows the condemned arriving in groups; this ayah has Hell's gates opened and commands them to enter, completing the opposite destination to 39:73.

The section explicitly warns that the proper name ʿĀd does not itself mean return, while its root note defines the true return; here عاد is an actual return to usury after warning, a relapse into wealth-seeking rather than the final return to God.
